summary: This informational document defines the xml2rfc version 3 vocabulary, an XML-based language for writing RFCs and Internet-Drafts. It is heavily derived from the version 2 vocabulary and obsoletes the v2 grammar described in RFC 7749.

plainLanguage.summary: Authors write RFCs with special tags, like instructions for a typesetter. This is the second edition of the tag list, with a few improvements.

subtitle: The XML tag set that authors use to write RFCs and Internet-Drafts, in its third edition.

tldr.problem: RFC and Internet-Draft authors write in an XML language called xml2rfc. Version 2 had awkward lists, tables and character formatting, and its grammar was written as a DTD.
tldr.mechanism: Version 3 keeps most of the v2 vocabulary and adds new elements such as lists with li, HTML-like tables, inline formatting, sourcecode and relref. It defines the grammar in RELAX NG and describes the tools (prep tool, formatters) expected to process documents.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7991 obsoletes the v2 grammar in RFC 7749. It is Informational, warns that later versions may change incompatibly, and has itself since been updated by RFC 9920.

today: RFC 7991 is an Informational document that obsoletes RFC 7749, and it has since been updated by RFC 9920. The RFC itself says later revisions may make non-interoperable changes.

sections.title: What xml2rfc v3 Is
sections.content:
RFC 7991 describes version 3 ("v3") of the xml2rfc vocabulary, an XML-based language used for writing RFCs and Internet-Drafts. It obsoletes the version 2 vocabulary in RFC 7749, which in turn obsoleted the original v1 in RFC 2629. Where possible, text is copied directly from RFC 7749.

The v3 format is meant to be used as part of the new RFC Series format described in RFC 6949. That format is expected to be handled by one or more new tools that prepare the XML and convert it to other representations. The RFC uses the word format for types of documents such as XML and HTML, and representation for a specific instance, such as an HTML document produced from an XML document.

Some constructs in the vocabulary may not appear in the final text at all. They can still carry useful data for index generation, a keyword database or syntax checks.

The RFC warns that non-interoperable changes in later versions are likely, based on experience with the new toolsets. Other implementers must not expect those changes to stay backwards-compatible with this document.
sections.plainLanguage: People who write RFCs type them using a markup language, like writing a web page. This document lists the tags you are allowed to use.

sections.title: What Changed from v2
sections.content:
The design criteria were that starting and editing a v3 document should be easier than in v2, that good v2-to-v3 conversion tools should exist, and that there were no current plans to make v3 XML the required submission format for drafts or RFCs. The RFC says it would rather encourage backwards compatibility than be constrained by it, but ease of use matters more. v3 is upwards compatible with v2, so a v2 document is meant to be a valid v3 document too.

New elements include <dl>, <ul> and <ol> lists whose children are <li>; character formatting with <strong>, <em>, <tt>, <sub> and <sup>; <aside>; <sourcecode> (separate from <artwork>); HTML-like tables; <blockquote>; <name>; <displayreference>; <refcontent>; <referencegroup>; <relref>; <link>; <br>; and <svg>.

New attributes include sortRefs, symRefs, tocDepth and tocInclude on <rfc>, which replace processing instructions that v2 used, plus ascii variants of several name and address fields so authors can give their native script as the main entry. Many block elements gain an anchor attribute for linking.

Other changes include allowing non-ASCII characters (the exact set is up to the RFC Series Editor), allowing <artwork> and <sourcecode> directly in a <section>, and making <t> contain only non-block elements. The grammar is no longer generated from a DTD but taken directly from the RELAX NG grammar.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a new edition of a rulebook. Most rules stay the same so old games still work, but there are new pieces for things people kept wanting to do, and a few clumsy old pieces are put on the shelf.

sections.title: Elements and Attributes
sections.content:
Section 2 describes every element and its attributes, one element per subsection, in alphabetical order from <abstract> to <xref>. Attributes are optional unless labeled mandatory. The vocabulary itself is defined in prose, backed by a RELAX NG schema in Appendix C, which can be used for automated validity checks. Some constraints exist only in prose, such as when the abbrev attribute is required.

The root element is <rfc>. It holds optional <link> elements, one <front>, one <middle> and an optional <back>. A <section> is a section inside <middle> or an appendix inside <back>, and subsections come from nesting sections.

Some <rfc> attributes steer formatters: tocInclude (default true), tocDepth (default 3), symRefs (default true, so references look like [RFC2119] rather than [3]) and sortRefs (default false). A <seriesInfo> element inside <front> says which series the document is in; a tool tells an RFC from an Internet-Draft by its name value of "RFC" or "Internet-Draft".

Whitespace is collapsed to a single space everywhere except inside <artwork> and <sourcecode>, and tab characters are prohibited in those two. Every element may carry xml:lang, xml:base, or both. Section 3 then lists the v2 elements that are deprecated, and Section 4 notes that SVG is covered in RFC 7996.
sections.plainLanguage: The big middle of the document is an alphabetical dictionary of tags. Each entry says what the tag is for, where it may go, and which settings it accepts.

sections.title: Anchors, Cross-References and Numbers
sections.content:
Many elements take an optional anchor attribute: a document-wide unique identifier that must be a valid XML Name limited to US-ASCII characters. Authors point at anchors with <xref target='...'/>. The target is mandatory and must match the anchor of some element, otherwise it is an error. The format attribute chooses how the reference reads: counter gives just a number, default gives text like "Section 2", and title gives the target's name. The value none is deprecated.

Readers, on the other hand, often want to point at parts of someone else's document that have no anchor. For that, processing tools add a pn attribute to many elements, generated automatically. Values follow fixed patterns, such as s-2.1.3 for a section, f-5 for a figure, t-5 for a table and p-2.1.3-7 for the seventh part number in a section.

Because anchors and generated values both become id attributes in HTML, they must not overlap. The simplest rule the RFC gives is not to choose an anchor that starts with a single letter followed by a hyphen. If an anchor does overlap, the processing tool rejects the document. The <relref> element, new in v3, lets an author reference a specific section or anchor inside a reference.
sections.plainLanguage: An anchor is a sticker you put on a page so you can say "see the sticker called overview". Tools also put numbered stickers on everything else, so nobody may reuse those sticker names.

sections.title: Processing Tools and XInclude
sections.content:
Appendix B describes the tools expected to handle v3. A prep tool checks a v3 document, adds and changes many attribute values, and produces a "prepared document" that is itself valid v3. It is described in RFC 7998 and is expected to have several modes: RFC mode for the RFC Editor, draft mode for the Internet-Draft submission tool, a diagnostic mode for authors, and a consolidation mode that produces output needing no external resources. Formatters then create HTML, PDF, plain text and possibly other outputs, normally from prepared documents.

Some attributes are controlled by the prep tool, for example pn, originalSrc, slugifiedName, derivedLink, derivedContent, and on <rfc> the attributes expiresDate, mode and scripts. The RFC says it is explicitly unsafe for an author to include these and expect the values to survive.

All tools for v3 are expected to support XInclude, written as <xi:include>, which needs the xi namespace declared on <rfc>. It is most often used to pull in references already formed as XML, and it can be used anywhere an XML element could be, but not where free text is used. In general XInclude should be used instead of ENTITY references and processing instructions that allow external inclusion.
sections.plainLanguage: A checker tool tidies and numbers your document first, and then printer tools turn it into web pages, PDFs or plain text. You can also glue in pieces of other files, like pasting in a shared paragraph.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The risks come from tools that read the XML. The name attribute of <artwork> can be used to derive a filename for saving to a local file system, and trusting that without pre-processing is a known risk (the RFC points to RFC 6266). The src attribute can be used to read files from the local system, so tools must not accept dangerous values, especially absolute references outside the current directory.

The type attribute of <artwork> and <sourcecode> encourages formatters to extract known kinds of content. Rendering or executing that extracted content without sanity checks is called "clearly a terrible idea". When there is an external URL, a processor or renderer should fetch the content into a sandbox so that it has only a localized impact. The security considerations for XML processing in RFC 3470 also apply.

The document also has an Internationalization section: because the format is based on XML it can represent arbitrary Unicode, though the RFC Series Editor may restrict characters in a particular RFC (see RFC 7997).
sections.plainLanguage: If a tool blindly trusts a file name or a path written inside a document, a sneaky author could make it overwrite or read files it should not. So tools must check first and do risky things in a closed-off sandbox.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
This document updates the registration of the Internet Media Type application/rfc+xml from the one in RFC 7749. It has no required parameters and one optional charset parameter with the same meaning as for application/xml. The file extension is .xml, or .rfcxml when disambiguation from other XML files is needed. The registration notes that different implementations of the format have had interoperability issues and that this publication is not expected to fix them.

IANA also registered a new link relation, convertedFrom, meaning that the linked document was later converted into the document that holds the link. For example, an RFC can link to the Internet-Draft that became the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: The document asks the official registry to give this kind of file its own label, so computers know it is an RFC written in XML, and to add a label for "this was converted from that".
